rows.verified: A confined space is enclosed or largely enclosed and has a reasonably foreseeable specified risk such as fire, explosion, loss of consciousness, asphyxiation or drowning.
Confined-space hazards can include noxious fumes, reduced oxygen, fire, flooding, drowning and engulfment by dust, grain or other contaminants.
Work in a confined space should be avoided wherever reasonably practicable.
Where entry cannot be avoided, the particular confined space and task must be risk assessed before work starts.
Harmful fumes should be ventilated or removed where this is needed to control the risk.
Where liquids or gases could enter, isolation measures such as locking valves shut should be considered.
A safe system of work should identify the precautions, people, equipment and controls needed for the entry.
Emergency arrangements and rescue procedures must be planned before confined-space work begins.
The required controls depend on the actual atmosphere, contents, access, task and potential inflows in the specific space.
Confined-space guidance is task- and site-specific safety context and is not an exact parcel-level probability.
Dutyholders must prevent danger to workers in or near excavations.
A competent person should inspect excavation supports or battering at the start of each working shift.
Work should not proceed until the excavation is safe.
Planning information should include ground conditions, underground structures or watercourses and the location of existing services.
Temporary support and other precautions should be decided and available before digging starts.
Plant, vehicles and spoil should not be placed so close to excavation edges that they increase collapse risk.
Substantial barriers or equivalent edge protection should be provided where people could fall into an excavation.
Excavation should not start until underground-service risks have been identified and controlled.
No type of ground can be assumed to remain unsupported in every condition; water, loading and disturbance can materially change stability.
Excavation evidence is site-, soil- and works-specific and is not converted into an exact parcel-level safety probability.
Lifting operations involving lifting equipment must be properly planned by a competent person.
Lifting operations must be appropriately supervised and carried out in a safe manner.
The lifting plan should address foreseeable risks and identify the people and resources needed for safe completion.
Lifting equipment and accessories must have adequate strength and stability for the intended use.
Suspended loads should not pass over occupied areas where this can be avoided.
